entries.title: Why the North Korean women's football team is so good
entries.summary: North Korea's young footballers enter the U-20 World Cup in Poland as defending champions – the 2024 title was their third. Why is the isolated state so good at the game?
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

North Korea's young footballers enter the U-20 World Cup in Poland as defending champions – the 2024 title was their third. Why is the isolated state so good at the game?

A year ago, North Korea's women successfully defended their U-17 World Cup title after defeating the Netherlands 3-0 in Morocco. It was the fourth time that the country has won the competition.

Now the country's U-20 team enter the World Cup in Poland as defending champions, having won their third World Cup in 2024. North Korea's women have clearly cemented their status as the dominant force in women's youth football.

But what is it that makes a state that, according to the United Nations, "does not have any parallel in the contemporary world" so good at youth football?

"International sport is one of the few ways to demonstrate their sovereignty, existence and identity to the international community, so this type of big success, from their point of view, is an important occasion where they can wave their national flag in front of the international audience," Dr Jung Woo Lee, a senior lecturer in Sport and Leisure Policy at the University of Edinburgh, told DW.

"At the same time, domestically, North Korea often uses sport as their propaganda tool to glorify their leaders and also how great their country is."

A clear and conscious strategy

Football is popular in the country, but recognizing that the gap to the top in senior football is much harder to close than in youth football, North Korea's leaders turned to women's youth football, where the gap is more manageable. It's also why success at this level hasn't benefited the senior team over the years. This strategy is not about pathways. It's about winning.

"The gap between established and developing clubs is also high because in many European countries, there is a professional league, and they get more support from a number of different stakeholders," Lee said.

"In youth football, I think European sport organizations highlight more on having fun when playing football. Whereas in North Korea, even if you are 13 or 14 years old, they join very highly disciplined, highly systematic and highly professionalized training regimes, so in early ages they can excel."

In Morocco, North Korea's U-17 team only conceded three goals in the entire tournament, and scored three or more on four occasions. This was a continuation of their form the year before, while the U-20 women in 2024 not only beat Argentina 6-2 but also secured three straight 1-0 victories from the quarterfinals onwards to win the tournament.

With the help of the Pyongyang International Football School where young girls are selected, developed and educated following a highly disciplined and scientific approach, North Korea has seen an opportunity and taken it.

Regime positioning, life-changing rewards

In the eyes of North Korea, this is also a victory for the communist regime.

"You need to remember that North Korea still maintains a very strong socialist and communist regime," Lee explained. "Particularly under Kim Jong Un, they try to compare capitalist and communist regimes and show the communist regime as superior to the capitalist. Also, when I look at some of the news reports about the North Korean performance in North Korean media, they highlighted that because they are (under) the communist regime, they do whatever they can, even if they're physically exhausted.

"Then they directly compare those mentalities with capitalist countries. In capitalism, when athletes are physically exhausted and injured, there is no way to perform. They need to be changed by their coach. But in socialist systems their will is more important than (a) professional opinion from the coach or any medical staff. So North Korea frames that as a superior system."

That psychological element has seemingly given the team an edge, but beyond a strong sense of patriotism and years of disciplined work lies the motivation of a life-changing reward.

"Although we often see North Korea as quite underdeveloped and very much agricultural and people experiencing hardship, those living in Pyongyang are quite different. They are kind of special," Lee explained.

As an incentive, he said, the regime can give players living outside the capital residence certificates, which are required to enter Pyongyang. At the same time, many players have been given apartments.

This motivation is not to be underestimated. Life in rural North Korea is tough, with shortages in food and health care reportedly common. Living in the big city is quite different.

"This is a way to change their life. It's kind of winning a lottery in a way," Lee explained.

What next for talented generation?

For star players such as Yu Jong-hyang, topscorer at the 2025 U-17 World Cup, or Choe Il-son, a key player in both U-17 and U-20 World Cup victories in 2024, the instinctive reaction is to wonder which WSL(English top division) or NWSL(US top division)  team will be trying to sign her, but that would be to forget the context in which she both lives and plays.

"I don't think it's impossible, but not so easy," Lee said of the idea of either stars playing abroad.

"First of all, (there are) the economic sanctions now imposed on North Korea," he said. "And also, whenever North Korean players joined a European league — there were a few occasions in basketball where any salary was not sent to the individual account of the players or the agent, but it goes to North Korea's government account, so I think that's another complexity involved."

While much about this team, like the country, remains a mystery, there is no denying that success at the youth level has always been the plan.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

This article was originally published on September 9, 2024. It was updated on November 9, 2025 to reflect North Korea's U-17 World Cup title win. It was also updated on September 4, 2026 ahead of the kickoff of the U-20 World Cup in Poland.

entries.title: Germany: Police suspect sabotage after another device found
entries.summary: A suspicious object that could damage power lines has been found near a German substation for a third time this week. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published September 4, 2026last updated September 4, 2026

A suspicious object that could damage power lines has been found near a German substation for a third time this week. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police investigate after suspicious object found near Dormagen electricity substation
  • Saxony-Anhalt parties launch final campaign push ahead of Sunday vote
  • Volkswagen to shed 100,000 jobs by 2030

Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from Germanyon Friday, September 4.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section Open electrical cabinet sparks police operation at Lower Saxony substation

Open electrical cabinet sparks police operation at Lower Saxony substation

Early Friday morning, a police patrol spotted an open cabinet at a power substation in the village of Ganderkesee, near Bremen in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony.

The find comes amid three suspected acts of sabotage at different substations in Germany over the past week. 

The officer who spotted the open cabinet called in additional personnel, a police spokesperson said Friday.

"Due to the special significance of the technical facility, the premises were immediately and thoroughly searched," the spokeswoman wrote.

No damage or unauthorized persons were found at the location.

"At no time was there any danger to the public," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, police near the western German city of Aachen are searching an area near a power plant in Weisweiler after receiving a letter from a man claiming responsibility for attempted sabotages elsewhere in Germany this week, and naming Weisweiler as a potential target.

Police have not said whether the man's claims are credible, nor whether any suspicious objects have been found during Friday morning's search.

Skip next section Germany's Zverev reaches third round of US Open

Germany's Zverev reaches third round of US Open

German tennis player Alexander Zverev came out on top after after a five-set clash with France's Quentin Halys at the US Open .

The four-hour 33-minute marathon at Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York City saw Zverev beat Halys 6-4, 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-7 (3), 6-3.

The match was the second in a row for Zverev ending after 2 a.m. following a first-round five-setter against 89th-ranked Lorenzo Sonego on Wednesday.

After the second-round win, 2026 French Open winner Zverev said he wasn't happy with his performance, "but I won, that's the most important thing."

"I'm winning ugly right now. It's also a skill to win ugly and when you're not playing great tennis. I think I've mastered that right now," he said.

"Physically, I feel fine. I am proud, I think, to be physically quite strong. I just hope at some point I'll start playing better tennis," Zverev added.

His next match is set for Saturday against Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Skip next section Suspects in Munich arson attack to appear in court

Suspects in Munich arson attack to appear in court

The Bavarian State Criminal Police Office (LKA) on Friday said a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man detained in connection with an arson attack in Munich are due to appear in court where a judge will decide whether to issue a formal arrest order.

Early Thursday morning, police were called to a fire at a construction site located near buildings in Munich's Berg am Laim neighborhood belonging to defense tech companies, including Helsing and Rohde & Schwarz.

Police said incendiary devices were thrown from a car. One was extinguished and did not cause any damage. Another was defused.

The suspects, both Bulgarian citizens, were arrested shortly after the incident at a nearby gas station. Police have not released any information about a possible motive.

Skip next section Volkswagen shares jump after 100,000 job cuts announced

Volkswagen shares jump after 100,000 job cuts announced

Markets on Friday responded positively after German automobile giant Volkswagen announced a major restructure that averted an escalation with unions and shareholder ​Lower ‌Saxony.

The carmaker announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed.

Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

Skip next section Parties in Saxony-Anhalt hold final campaign events ahead of Sunday's polls

Parties in Saxony-Anhalt hold final campaign events ahead of Sunday's polls

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt goes to the polls on Sunday, and several parties are holding closing rallies on Friday to drum up support among undecided voters.

According to a survey by polling group "Forschungsgruppe Wahlen" cited by DPA news agency, 31% of respondents are still undecided.

Polls are showing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the lead as it aims for an a absolute majority that would allow it to lead a state government in Germany for the first time. 

The AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and national party chairman Tino Chrupalla are due at a campaign event in the state capital, Magdeburg.

Sven Schulze, currently state premierand lead candidate for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also has engagements in Magdeburg planned for Friday.

The Left Party's lead candidate Eva von Angern is appearing in Magdeburg, and the city of Halle, alongside leading party figures Heidi Reichinnek, Gregor Gysi and Dietmar Bartsch.

The Greens are planning events in Halle and Naumburg, with lead candidate Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz joined by federal party chairman Felix Banaszak.

Saxony-Anhalt's current coalition government, comprising the CDU, center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP),  is set to lose its majority, according to polls.

Skip next section 'Suspicious objects' found near substation in Lower Saxony: reports

'Suspicious objects' found near substation in Lower Saxony: reports

In the northwestern region of Lower Saxony, police are investigating "suspicious objects" found in the pre-dawn hours Friday morning at a power substation near the small town of Ganderkesee outside of Bremen, the Bild tabloid reported.

"A discovery was made that required a police investigation," a police spokeswoman was quoted by the newspaper as saying. A helicopter had been called in to illuminate the area from above.

No further details were immediately available.

Skip next section Police suspect another sabotage attempt near Dormagen substation

Police suspect another sabotage attempt near Dormagen substation

Police in western Germany say a suspicious device found at an electricity substation in the small city of Dormagen between Cologne and Düsseldorf was likely intended to "cause damage."

"Someone apparently tried to deliberately cause a short circuit," a Cologne police spokesperson told AFP news agency.

The object was discovered late Thursday by a passer-by. A police spokesperson said it may have been a "suspicious launching device."

The Bild tabloid reported that homemade rockets with launching devices, including timers and cooper wires, were discovered. Police have not confirmed the report.

The new discovery Friday is the latest this week in what police say are attempts at damaging critical infrastructure. 

The first incident on Tuesday near the Jänschwalde coal power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg involved homemade projectiles resembling New Year's Eve fireworks that can short out high-voltage power lines by shooting a grounding wire over them.

A day later, similar objects were found near a power station in Bergheim, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

A number of suspicious devices have been found near German power infrastructure this week, with a third incident overnight in Dormagen being treated by police as a likely sabotage attempt.

No significant damage has been reported in any of the cases and police have not revealed any suspects.

Meanwhile, parties in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt are holding their final campaign events ahead of a state election on Sunday that could see the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) come out on top.

Stay with us as we bring you the latest developments on these stories and more.

entries.title: India launches first ever imaging satellite into geo orbit
entries.summary: The newly launched satellite will hover some 36,000 kilometers above Earth and is being called India's "eye in the sky." DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Published September 4, 2026last updated September 4, 2026

The newly launched satellite will hover some 36,000 kilometers above Earth and is being called India's "eye in the sky." DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India has carried out a successful launch of its EOS-05 Earth observation satellite
  • India ace Smriti Mandhana is now the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket

  • Air India begins voluntary testing for all its pilots after probe agency finds drug test of a captain "non-negative" in August air incident

 Here is a roundup of the latest developments from India on Friday, September 4.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Air India probe flags triple hydraulic loss, pilot drug test

Air India probe flags triple hydraulic loss, pilot drug test

An Air India plane which experienced a sudden drop in altitude while flying from Phuket to New Delhi last month suffered a temporary loss of hydraulic systems, Indian investigators have said.

The plane's pilot also returned a "non-negative" result in a confirmatory ⁠test ​for psychoactive substances, India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) said in a preliminary report on Friday.

The body is probing the incident involving the Air India A320 flight, which plummeted 300 feet (91 meters) on August 4 while cruising over the Indian state of Odisha, before recovering and landing safely in Delhi.

A total of 20 passengers and four crew members were injured.

Following the incident, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

On Friday, the AAIB, updated the event, which was earlier classified as a "serious incident" to an "accident."

What did the probe agency say?

The AAIB said that the flight-control system detected the loss of all three of the aircraft's hydraulic systems for several seconds.

"The aircraft encountered altitude upset," it said in the report, adding that the plane gained 372 feet initially and fell by 292 feet.

A two-second stall warning came after the hydraulic failure, disengaging the autopilot and setting off ​a continuous cockpit alarm, the report said.

The stall warning came when the seatbelt signs were off and the rapid pitch up and down threw those on board against the overhead bins, leading to the injuries, the report elaborated.

"Subsequently, the aircraft operation returned to its normal operating condition," the agency's report said.

The report went on to add that the pilot-in-command returned a "non-negative" test for psychoactive substances.

"The confirmation of use of psychoactive substance is a serious concern," it said without identifying the substance.

What has Air India said?

Following Friday's report, Air India released a statement saying that it had started voluntary testing of "100% of its pilots" after the incident as "a further step to reinforce its safety-first approach."

"We acknowledge the release of the preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) and continue to extend our full cooperation to the investigation, including providing access to all relevant operational, maintenance and technical records," the Indian flag carrier said.

Skip next section Smriti Mandhana becomes women's international cricket's leading run-scorer

Smriti Mandhana becomes women's international cricket's leading run-scorer

India vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has smashed records to become the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket.

Mandhana's total runs now stand at 10,880 as she surpassed former India captain Mithali Raj'srally of ‌10,868 ⁠runs on the international scoreboard.

Madhana achieved the feat as she knocked out a century during team India's win against Hong Kong in the Women's Asia Cup on Thursday.

The ton, which was Madhana's 18th international hundred, also marked the most centuries by a player in women's international cricket.

"I didn't know all of this happened," the 30-year-old left hander said after scripting history.

"But I ‌love batting and am happy to contribute. There are ‌days ​when you hit balls from the stumps. There are days when you edge one. It's extremely unpredictable."

Former record-holder Raj has congratulated Mandhana.

"To see you go past my record and become the highest run-scorer in international cricket is a moment I'm genuinely proud of. Here's to many more runs and milestones. Keep going!" she wrote on X.

Skip next section India launches key Earth observation satellite

India launches key Earth observation satellite

The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) on Friday successfully deployed the country's first ever imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit.

A Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) —  carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite — lifted off from ISRO's primary spaceport, the Satish Dhawan Space Center in Sriharikota, at 2:55 a.m. local time (2125 UTC).

The Indian space agency shared visuals of the countdown for the launch which ended with the GSLV-F17 firing up and lifting off, lighting up the dark early morning skies in its wake.

About 18 minutes later, ISRO announced that the satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit.

ISRO proclaimed "Mission Success!" in a post on X.

ISRO's first success in 2026

The launch marked the 19th flight of India's GSLV. It was also ISRO's first success this year after a mission setback in January saw a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle rocket failing to place 16 satellites in the intended orbit

The EOS-05 — with a payload of over 2,300 kilograms — is the country's heaviest ever satellite to be carried by a GSLV.

The satellite — dubbed as India's "eye in the sky" — will operate from an altitude of roughly 36,000 kilometers above Earth, which is higher than typical low-Earth-orbit observation satellites

The satellite will match the home planet's rotational speed.

Its expected mandate is to bolster India's ability to obtain frequent imagery of large areas for applications including Earth observation and monitoring.

"The health of the satellite is perfectly alright," ISRO Chairman V Narayanan said after the launch.

PM Modi lauds India's growing space capabilities

On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the satellite's launch as "yet another outstanding achievement" by the Indian space agency and "a proud moment" for the country.

"The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India's first-ever imaging satellite from Geosynchronous orbit is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India's space sector," he said on X.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Friday edition of the India news blog, where we give you a round up of all the biggest headlines that have got people talking across the country.

In the early hours of the morning, India successfully launched its first ever imaging satellite in the geosynchronous orbit, etching a milestone in the country's space program.

Another feat was notched — this time in the world of cricket — as India batter Smriti Mandhana became the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket.

Meanwhile, in diplomatic news, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar has wrapped up a visit to Kyiv that came amid India's renewed push for peace in Russia's war in Ukraine.

Follow along as we bring you more.

entries.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
entries.summary: The motto of this year's festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.
entries.content:
Germany

2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home

September 4, 2026

The motto of this year's festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.

Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle.

The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert on September 4.

For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explains, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics." He adds: "We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure." This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, András Schiff, to perform at the festival this year.

A musical home for everyone



The new hall is not only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too. Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed "Festival Salon" where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall.

The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music.

"For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," says festival director Steven Walter. who has lived in various places around the world himself. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections."

Beethoven reinterpreted

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate it, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos.

The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A life." Even so, Caeyers says he is far from finished discovering the composer.

"Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Pianist Kit Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today."

Spotlight on Georgia

This year's Beethovenfest artists will introduce music from their homelands. Among them are Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga and Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war.

Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year.

As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music being performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace").

Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course.

17-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze is regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents. He was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work.

Beyond classical music

Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music.

American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age. "We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," says Philipp Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music."

The Beethovenfest runs from Sept 3 through Oct 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Meloni government becomes longest-serving in postwar Italy
entries.summary: The hard-right government has officially beaten the record set by media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi. Meloni and her party are using the opportunity to celebrate and also rally for the 2027 election.
entries.content:
Italy

Meloni government becomes longest-serving in postwar Italy

September 4, 2026

The hard-right government has officially beaten the record set by media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi. Meloni and her party are using the opportunity to celebrate and also rally for the 2027 election.

The right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni on Friday became the longest-serving since the Italian Republic was established 80 years ago.

Meloni's government, the most-right wing to have ruled Italy since World War II, has been in charge for 1,413 days.

That's one day more than billionaire media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi, who still holds the record for collectively serving longest as prime minister with nine years in office, albeit under different governments.

Since Italy became a republic after the end of the war, it has had 68 governments within 80 years, with governments lasting around 13 months on average.

How is Meloni celebrating her record tenure?

Meloni and her far-right Brothers of Italy (Fdl) party are planning a celebration on Friday in the port city of Bari in the southern Puglia region.

Some 80 coaches will transport supporters there, with Meloni due to address the gathering in the evening.

Deputy Prime Ministers Matteo Salvini and Antonio Tajani are also due to appear via video link. The event is effectively an opportunity to campaign for Italy's 2027 election.

What does the Meloni government and its supporters say?

The Meloni government boasts one million extra people in employment in its four years in power, unemployment below 6% as well as a €21 billion ($24 billion) reduction in personal income taxes.

They are also especially proud of what they say is a sharp decline in migrant arrivals.

The prime minister, whose party has neo-Fascist roots, also says Italy's influence on the world stage has grown.

Meloni's nationalist streak was celebrated at home on more than one occasion. One notable example was when US President Donald Trump, with whom the Italian leader had initially and unusually enjoyed a cordial relationship, said she had begged him for a photo.

"Italy doesn't beg," Meloni said of Trump's claim, much to the satisfaction of many Italians.

What do Meloni's critics say?

Critics of Italy's first female prime minister and her longest-serving government however argue that despite the numbers, the country's persistent problems remain.

They list weak productivity, demographic decline and long-standing inefficiencies in healthcare, education and public administration. The rising cost of living is also a major criticism.

"Have wages increased? No. Petrol costs more, job insecurity has increased, people are retiring less and the healthcare system is functioning less effectively," Maurizio Landini, head of the CGIL trade union, said ahead of the celebrations.

Parallel to the Meloni party in Bari, her opponents are also planning a gathering across the city. Organizers accuse her government of creating a "war and weapons economy" and a "police state," as well as fueling a climate of hate against migrants.

Meanwhile, others think the prime minister strayed from her election campaign and has become too moderate, including a potential challenger in the coming vote.

Retired army general Roberto Vannacci, whose party is further to the far right than Meloni's, is known for hard-line positions on immigration and national identity.

Polls show his party has overtaken both the anti-immigrant League and right-wing Forza Italia parties, both members of Meloni's ruling coalition.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden
entries.summary: The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV onslaught?
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV onslaught?

Volkswagen has built one of the largest workforces in the global auto industry.

At nearly 630,000 people — 680,000 if you count joint ventures in China — VW employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, 140% more than Stellantis and nearly 240% more than Ford.

That headcount was once a sign of Germany's industrial might and VW's huge profits. Now, it's become a massive burden, one that's forcing the company to make painful job cuts to survive against agile Chinese competitors.

After already trimming thousands of positions last year as profits came under pressure, Volkswagen is now preparing to slash 50,000 additional jobs worldwide, including tens of thousands in Germany. The proposal got the backing of the VW Supervisory Board on Thursday, September 2.

VW also wants to close four German factories, a plan that the supervisory board on Thursday stopped short of agreeing to implement right away.

These cuts include VW luxury brands like Porsche and Audi. Other German automakers and suppliers are facing similar pressures. Mercedes-Benz is planning to cut several thousand jobs, and suppliers like Bosch have announced large cost savings.

How VW got to this point

Much of VW's headcount issue stems from long-standing strategic decisions.

Meghan Ostertag, an analyst for economic policy at the US-based Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, says VW's much larger workforce was needed because the firm chose to control more stages of production than its peers.

"The company makes many of its components and software internally, increasing the demand for labor and, of course, labor costs," Ostertag told DW, adding that factory expenses in Germany can be "up to twice those of the competition."

Other experts point to an aggressive acquisition strategy over the years, which brought brands including Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti into the VW fold — not to mention several truck makers.

"That strategy worked to some extent, but the complexities of integrating all those brands, supply chains and different designs make VW very complicated to operate," Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at the London-based Ultima Media, told DW.

Why the VW model broke

Although Volkswagen survived the 2015 Dieselgate emissions scandal without suffering lasting financial damage, the company incurred massive costs and soon faced a new set of problems.

The company was slow to transition its production to electric vehicles (EVs) — just as Chinese EV makers gained serious traction and a technological edge. That delay contributed to slower sales in China, which accounted for a third of total VW sales, as well as softening demand in Europe and other key markets.

VW also repeated a mistake made by the US auto industry decades earlier. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Big Three — Ford, GM, and Chrysler (now part of Stellantis) — were bloated and slow to adapt when Japanese and European competitors began eating into their market share.

By the time US carmakers shifted toward leaner production methods, a decade had passed, and they had fallen significantly behind, noted Ostertag.

Toyota, which produces a similar number of vehicles as VW, operates with nearly half as many workers by relying more on suppliers, higher automation and a simpler management structure.

In a research note, auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt pointed to another factor: the "stranglehold" that trade unions and a key shareholder have over VW. This, he said, had helped cause "years of neglect in readjusting workforce numbers."

The northern German state of Lower Saxony — home to Volkswagen's global headquarters in Wolfsburg — holds 20% of the company's voting rights, can veto major decisions, and has previously pressured executives not to close plants or lay off staff, notably during the Dieselgate and COVID supply chain crises. It's ramping up the pressure this time, too.

Over the decades, Germany's powerful unions, meanwhile, have repeatedly held out for high wage increases and generous benefits, which have made VW staff among the best-paid autoworkers in the world.

Is VW's turnaround plan enough?

Analysts warn that the company may have to cut more than the annual €4 billion the firm hopes to save to secure its future.

The current proposals to cut 50,000 additional jobs, they say, will bring savings and help improve short-term profitability. But VW's underlying cost base and slow decision-making culture mean deeper, more radical reforms may well be needed.

VW should "invest more heavily in automation," Ostertag told DW, adding that it would allow the carmaker to "better compete with leaner firms," such as China's BYD, one of the fastest-growing EV brands in Europe.

Analysts say VW has lagged peers in plant automation levels but has stepped up investments in robotics and digital upgrades for its EV production. The company is also planning its first sub-€20,000 EV next year.

With China responsible for around 30% of VW's global vehicle output, Harrison predicts more production shifts to Asia and the potential to share VW's European plants with Chinese EV producers, a move previously seen as "unthinkable."

German government, EU offer a lifeline

On the policy front, the German government is providing subsidies and loans for domestic EV battery plants to help reduce reliance on Chinese imports.

The European Union, meanwhile, is advancing the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA is meant to boost the bloc's competitiveness and shield strategic industries from unfair competition from China.

The EU has already imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese-made EVs. But they are far below the 100% levies that the US charges, which have largely shut Chinese competitors out of the US auto market.

Historian Niall Ferguson from Harvard University warned that Europe has been slow to respond to China's strategy of giving huge subsidies to EV makers that help undercut European rivals.

"Unless there's radical change, I predict: Europeans will be driving Chinese cars on a massive scale very soon," Ferguson told Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper earlier this year.

During the same interview, economist Moritz Schularick, President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, suggested using market access as leverage — only allowing Chinese brands to sell in Europe if they produce locally.

Schularick responded provocatively when questioned on VW's long-term future, predicting that Germany's auto giant would "likely be bought by a Chinese car maker like BYD."

Edited by: Ashutosh Pandey

Editor's note: The article, originally published on July 7, 2026, has been updated to include the VW Supervisory Board's backing for a restructuring plan calling for an additional 50,000 job cuts.

entries.title: Nepal: Two pulled alive from tunnel nine days after floods
entries.summary: Crews are racing to find hundreds more people still believed to be trapped after a glacier collapse triggered floods that killed more than 1,200 people.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal: Two pulled alive from tunnel nine days after floods

September 4, 2026

Crews are racing to find hundreds more people still believed to be trapped after a glacier collapse triggered floods that killed more than 1,200 people.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country's border region with China.

Emergency teams are continuing efforts to reach hundreds more believed trapped inside similar tunnels.

The men, identified as mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, were freed from the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station's tunnel along the Trishuli River, according to a statement from the office of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha.

"As long as there is breath, there is hope!" Shrestha said in a statement. "Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone's efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope."

What do we know about the rescue?

Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, authorities said.

Video and photos showed Maharjan, 45, pulled from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered. Images showed him being placed on a stretcher, while Shah, 30, whose face was covered in mud, was carried out on a worker's back to a rescue tent, where army doctors fitted him with an oxygen mask and checked his vitals.

An aide to the energy minister said Maharjan could not move his hands or legs, while Shah's injuries were not considered critical. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.

Family members reacted with relief. Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, told the Associated Press, "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," adding that the family was heading to the hospital to see him.

What is happening at the hydropower project sites?

These were the first successful rescues concerning the hydropower projects along the Trishuli River. Officials say as many as 900 workers remain missing across a number of project sites, with roughly 500 believed trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

At the Trishuli 3A project specifically, the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal put the number of missing workers at 557, with about 115 believed trapped in the main tunnel.

Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remained hopeful more survivors would be found: "We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," he said.

A team of experts coordinating through a WhatsApp group has been guiding rescue crews at the sites, becoming a key tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the search effort.

What is the scale of damage caused by the Nepal floods?

Separately, Nepal's disaster authority estimated the floods caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion, €2.20 billion) in damage to property, housing and infrastructure, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Reuters.

He said the first four months of early recovery — including rebuilding roads, setting up temporary shelters, and restoring water and power — would cost an estimated $52.6 million.

"These are estimated amounts. We have calculated this in coordination with different concerned agencies and departments," Upreti said, noting a more detailed assessment would follow. He said Nepal would need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-affected areas, with at least 7,500 destroyed outright.

The floods on August 26 were triggered by the collapse of a glacier upstream on the Trishuli River that sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through towns and villages near the Nepal-China border.

At least 1,259 people have been killed in Nepal, according to the country's disaster management agency, with more than 5,000 still missing.

China reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing on the Tibet side of the border as of late Wednesday.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Argentina: Milei reignites dispute over Falkland Islands
entries.summary: The Argentine leader said that a change in the US position on the Falkland Islands could be coming, which would alter Washington's years-long neutrality on the issue.
entries.content:
Argentina

Argentina: Milei reignites dispute over Falkland Islands

September 4, 2026

The Argentine leader said that a change in the US position on the Falkland Islands could be coming, which would alter Washington's years-long neutrality on the issue.

Argentine President Javier Milei said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands could be changing.

He added that his country would impose sanctions on any oil companies operating in the British overseas territory.

In a nationally televised speech on Thursday, Milei reiterated Argentina's stance that the Falkland Islands are part of its territory. This move could further escalate the long-standing dispute with Britain over the islands.

The Argentine leader also praised US President Donald Trump's comments regarding the US potentially revisiting its largely neutral position on the Falklands, saying this is a result of his close relationship with Trump.

According to Milei, the US is considering this change in position due to Argentina being a "reliable partner, aligned with Western values" that can be "a valuable ally in the decades to come."

Milei announced several moves aimed at stopping the Sea Lion oil project, which is located about 140 miles from the islands — an area that Argentina considers its own. Two companies, one from the UK and one from Israel, plan to begin drilling in the area in the coming months with the goal of producing oil by 2028.

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Milei said, adding that any further advance on the Islands will be viewed as a "violation of our national security."

The Falklands issue is a point of consensus in an Argentine society divided by political differences in other areas.

Britain 'unwavering' position unchanged

Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson said the British government's position was "long-standing and unwavering."

"Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount,” he said.

Any change in the US' neutral approach towards the dispute between Britain and Argentina would be a major shift and could contribute to further deterioration in already strained transatlantic relations.

Asked about whether his administration could change its position on the Falkland Islands, Trump said he "always" reviews positions.

"That's just one of many," he added.

In another interview, Trump was asked whether the US would come to help Britain should it be involved in an armed conflict over the islands.

"Your country was not there to help me," he answered, referring to Britain's refusal to take an active part in the joint US-Israeli campaign against Iran.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' against Infantino
entries.summary: The dispute between the two football associations reached a US court, in which UEFA is looking for permission to collect evidence for criminal proceedings in Switzerland.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' against Infantino

September 4, 2026

The dispute between the two football associations reached a US court, in which UEFA is looking for permission to collect evidence for criminal proceedings in Switzerland.

World football governing body FIFA took a lash at Europe's UEFA for starting a "smear campaign" and "fishing expedition" against FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino.

This comes after a dispute between the two organizations due to FIFA's plan to sell a stake in its commercial rights, with UEFA submitting an ex parte application to the US District Court in New York to obtain testimony and documents from US-based entities. These documents will be used in potential criminal proceedings in Switzerland, where both FIFA and UEFA are based.

"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA’s smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership,” FIFA said in a filing in US District Court in Colorado on Thursday.

FIFA's filing in Colorado was a motion to intervene, requesting that the discovery process be postponed or dismissed.

According to UEFA, the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), an entity which would have had the commercial rights linked over the FIFA World Cup to investors was developed without adequate consulting FIFA's 211 member associations, as well as FIFA's own governing bodies.

UEFA threatened to boycott the FIFA World Cup should the move go ahead.

The move would have affected both the men's and the women's tournaments.

FIFA argued that the association representing European football had tried to scupper the proposal with a bid to keep European football's dominance as is.

Demands for Infatino's resignation

Pressure has been mounting on both FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino since the FFE plans were made public.

This resulted in several countries saying they will not support Infantino's reelection for a fourth term as president in March 2027, when the Swiss-born FIFA boss looks for a fourth term in office.

Aside from UEFA, two other continental confederations demand Infantino's resignation.

Both CONCACAF, representing North and Central America and the Caribbean, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) voiced their objections to Infantino. Only the South American and African confederations still support him.

UEFA also demanded a "genuinely independent external review" of how the proposal came about.

"FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community to simply accept its conclusions," UEFA said.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
entries.summary: The company will carry out the biggest job cuts ever seen in the industry. Volkswagen also plans to restructure and invest in research.
entries.content:
Germany

Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade

September 4, 2026

The company will carry out the biggest job cuts ever seen in the industry. Volkswagen also plans to restructure and invest in research.

German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

'The motor of the entire region'

What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

"If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency.

"The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region."

Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.

Company reforms to drive profitability

However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South.

The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive.

Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third.
